seen-1.text:
Nakshi Kantha is a kind of embroidered quilt. The name was taken from the Bangla word, 'naksha' which means artistic pattern. It is a kind of traditional craft and is said to be indigenous to Bangladesh and West Bengal in India. The art has been practised in rural Bangladesh for centuries. The name Nakshi Kantha became popular after the poet Jasimuddin's poem 'Nakshi Kanthar Math' was published in 1929.
Traditional kanthas are made for family use. Old or new cloth and thread are used to make these quilts. Mymensingh, Jamalpur, Rajshahi, Faridpur, Bogura and Jashore are most famous for this craft. Now, it is produced commercially. You can find them in many expensive handicraft shops in cities. The quilts are now in great demand because of the colourful patterns and designs embroidered on them.

seen-2.text:
People’s music, also known as folk music, consists of tunes, lyrics, and knowledge passed down orally for generations. Over time, this music has evolved, closely tied to the way people live. Our agriculture, food, ecology, seasons, and rituals are all reflected in these songs. Palligiti, Bhatiwali, Jari, Sari, Gambhira, Lalon Giti, Paalagan, and the songs of Hason Raja all embody the self-expression of the people.
As the landscape changes, the music shifts too. In the hill tracts, you encounter music with the same role but expressed in the diverse languages of the ethnic communities. The instruments used for folk music are crafted from materials found in the surroundings—animal skin, bamboo, and calabash are common examples. The sounds they produce are deeply connected to the land they come from. As people migrate to cities and villages transform, these traditional tunes are slowly fading. However, folk music still finds its place in mainstream films and music albums.

textbook-poems.text:
Translation of Hason Raja’s song “Loke Bole Bole Re (Oh, They Say)”
Oh, They say my house is no good,
But what can I build with nothing here?
I’ll erect a home,
Yet how long will I truly stay?
I gaze into the mirror,
Noticing the strands of grey in my hair:
Thinking of this,
Hason Raja never built a dwelling.
Where will Allah take him? Where will he find rest?
This uncertainty brings him to tears.
If only Hason Raja had known his days,
He would have painted his rooms in vibrant hues.
Oh, They say my house is no good,
But what can I build with nothing here?

Excerpt from ‘The Field of the Embroidered Quilt’ (Nokshi Kanthar Math) by Jasimuddin; translation E. M. Milford
Spreading the embroidered quilt,
She works the livelong night,
As if her poet were
On his bereaved plight.
Many a joy and many a sorrow
Is written on her breast;
The story of Rupai’s life is there,
Line by line expressed.
“How will he bear the pain, mother?
On this quilt lies all of mine—
All my pain and my grief,
Embroidered line by line.
So lay it on my grave, mother.
This picture of my grief,
That his and mine upon its breast
May mingling find relief.

The following is a fictional account of a neighbourhood reading project. In January 2026, a group of young volunteers opened a weekend reading corner in a community centre. They began with sixty donated books and two tables. A retired teacher, Mr Hasan, helped them arrange the books by subject. The centre opened every Friday from three to six in the afternoon. Children could read there without paying a fee. Older students took turns reading stories aloud to younger visitors. By April, the collection had grown to one hundred books. The volunteers kept a register to record which titles were most popular. They discovered that illustrated science books attracted many readers. Instead of buying expensive decorations, they used their small fund to repair damaged books. Their next plan was to organise a monthly book discussion for families.

tasks.instruction:
Read the opening and complete the story A Helpful Decision in at least ten new sentences. Give a suitable title.
Arefin was returning from the market when he saw an elderly man standing beside a broken bicycle. Dark clouds were gathering overhead...
tasks.answer:
A Helpful Decision
Arefin stopped and asked the man what had happened. The chain had slipped, and the man could not repair it alone. Arefin had seen his brother fix the same problem before. He asked permission to examine the bicycle. After moving it to a safe place beside the road, he carefully put the chain back. The man thanked him, but the tyre was also losing air. Arefin remembered a repair shop a short distance away. He offered to walk there with the man. They reached the shop just before the rain began. The mechanic repaired the tyre while they waited under the roof. The man offered Arefin some money for his help. Arefin politely declined and said that he was happy to have been useful. He returned home later than expected and explained everything to his mother. She reminded him that kindness should be joined with sensible attention to safety.

tasks.instruction: Write a paragraph on Preserving Our Folk Culture in about 150 words.
tasks.answer: Preserving Our Folk Culture means keeping valuable traditions alive while allowing people to express themselves in new ways. Folk songs, crafts, stories and festivals connect us with earlier generations. They show how people have worked, celebrated and understood their surroundings. In Bangladesh, an embroidered quilt or a traditional song can carry memories that an ordinary written record does not contain. However, changes in work and living places may make some practices less common. Young people can help by learning from skilled craft workers, listening respectfully to older musicians and recording stories with permission. Schools can arrange demonstrations and discussions without turning every tradition into an expensive show. Buying fairly priced local crafts can also support the people who make them. Preservation does not mean forcing everyone to live exactly as people did in the past. It means understanding the value of traditions and giving their practitioners opportunities to continue. A living culture grows stronger when knowledge is shared with care and respect.

tasks.instruction: Write a dialogue between two friends about the importance of learning English.
tasks.answer:
Sumona: Why do you think learning English is important, Ananya?
Ananya: It helps us communicate with people from many countries and use a wide range of books and educational materials.
Sumona: I can read simple texts, but I feel nervous when speaking.
Ananya: That is common. We can practise short conversations without laughing at each other’s mistakes.
Sumona: Should we memorise long speeches?
Ananya: Understanding and regular practice are more useful than repeating words without knowing their meaning.
Sumona: What can we do after class?
Ananya: We can read a short passage, note useful expressions and discuss what it says.
Sumona: Could listening help too?
Ananya: Yes. Suitable programmes can help us notice pronunciation and natural expressions. We should choose materials we can understand.
Sumona: Does learning English mean neglecting Bangla?
Ananya: Not at all. We can value our mother tongue while learning another language.
Sumona: Let us practise for ten minutes every day.
Ananya: Agreed. Small, steady efforts can build confidence.
